answer: The submission is honest and well-structured, but it reads as an idea-stage concept paper rather than a persuasive venture case. Key improvements: (1) Quantify the problem and market. Replace 'several million' and 'a meaningful portion' with cited figures (e.g., percent of 18-34 chronic-condition patients who skip doses due to cost, size of the cohort, a bottom-up TAM/SAM/SOM, and the realistic campus-region beachhead). (2) Show evidence of demand, not just a prototype. Report concrete pilot metrics: number of users, interviews conducted, average savings found per prescription, repeat usage, and direct quotes. Even small-sample numbers (e.g., '12 of 15 users found a cheaper price, median saving $X') are far stronger than 'early comments suggest.' (3) Build a real financial model. Define referral fee per fill, expected fills per user per month, CAC, free-to-paid conversion, premium price, and unit economics with a simple 12-24 month projection. Itemize the $75K ask by category and tie each tranche to a milestone (e.g., data licensing, pilot size, partner LOIs). Quantify the success target (e.g., 500 users, $X average monthly savings, 40% 90-day retention). (4) Address the core business model risk directly. Explain how a low-income, cost-sensitive segment generates referral revenue and how referral fees from discount providers avoid bias toward whoever pays most, since this threatens user trust and the 'compare across sources' differentiator. Show evidence of provider interest (conversations, LOIs, or at least outreach results). (5) Sharpen differentiation and defensibility. Current competitors (GoodRx-style apps, pharmacy and insurer apps) already offer comparison; 'young adult focus' and budgeting are thin moats. Articulate why this segment behaves differently, what proprietary data, workflow or distribution channel (campus health centers, clinics) creates a lasting advantage, and why incumbents would not simply add budgeting. (6) Address regulatory, privacy and data risk concretely. Health-related data raises HIPAA applicability questions, state privacy laws, data handling and security practices, and the licensing/accuracy of pricing data (coupon prices are volatile). State what you collect, what you do not, and your plan for compliance and liability, rather than only asking mentors for help. (7) Strengthen the team section. Highlight relevant traction and credibility; the team is all students with no healthcare, pharmacy or regulatory experience. Convert informal advisors (health policy faculty, pharmacist) into named advisors, and specify how the gaps will be filled. (8) Clarify go-to-market and customer acquisition. Describe a specific channel plan, expected conversion, and how you scale beyond one university region, including cost per acquired user. (9) Add a clear, prioritized milestone roadmap with dates and measurable gates, plus a short risk section (data accuracy, partner dependence, retention, regulatory) with mitigations. (10) Tighten the writing: lead with a one-line value proposition and a crisp traction summary, cut hedging language ('we have not yet...') in favor of 'here is our plan and how we will test it,' and use concrete numbers throughout. The shift needed is from describing intentions to demonstrating evidence, economics and a defensible path to revenue.
